name: Pressurized mesotherapy

lead:
Pressurized mesotherapy delivers the same kinds of cosmetic mixtures used in mesotherapy, such as vitamins, hyaluronic acid or plant extracts, without needles, by using an accelerated jet of air. It is offered for skin rejuvenation and for reducing small fat deposits.
The appearance goal is smoother, more hydrated skin or a slimmer local contour. One study reported that the pressurized method reduced fat layers more than needles did, though both showed reductions, and cosmetic uses of mesotherapy generally have not been tested in standard clinical trials.

paras: Treatments are done by providers in clinics or salons, who apply a solution and use the device to propel it into the skin. People who choose it usually cite avoiding injections.

Reports about mesotherapy include inflammation and swelling from some solutions, and infection clusters (skin abscesses and a mycobacterial infection in one Australian salon) tied to hygiene. France briefly banned mesotherapy for fat removal in 2011 before the ban was lifted after problems were linked to unhygienic conditions. Brazil and some other countries have restricted fat-removal use.

angle.text: It is marketed as a way to get mesotherapy's skin and contouring effects without injections. Claims rest mainly on small studies and case reports.

lead: Pressurized mesotherapy is a needle-free variant of mesotherapy in which an accelerated jet of air propels a solution into the skin instead of injecting it.[1] Mesotherapy itself involves intradermal or subcutaneous delivery of substances such as vitamins, enzymes, hyaluronic acid and plant extracts, with the stated aim of nourishing and hydrating skin, and sometimes dissolving fat.[1]

For looks, the intended payoff is skin rejuvenation or a reduced fat layer in a treated area. The method was founded by French physician Michel Pistor, the term was coined by the French press in 1958, and the French Academy of Medicine recognized mesotherapy as a specialty in 1987.[1]

Cosmetic uses of mesotherapy have not been tested in standard clinical trials, though case studies exist. One study cited on Wikipedia found that the pressurized approach reduced fat layers more than needles did, with both showing reductions.[1]

paras: Traditional mesotherapy uses small needles to place solutions in or beneath the skin. Pressurized mesotherapy replaces the needle with a pressurized air jet.[1]

Wikipedia describes mesotherapy as an alternative medicine technique with no proven clinical efficacy for its cosmetic aims and notes poor scientific backing. A prospective study of 10 patients who received facial multivitamin mesotherapy found no clinically relevant rejuvenation benefit.[1] Deoxycholic acid (Kybella), a separate approved injectable for under-chin fat, was tested in a trial of about 2,600 patients with a 68.2 percent response rate.[1]

Critics say the contents of mesotherapy mixtures are often unknown, and phosphatidylcholine can cause inflammation and swelling. Skin abscesses and a mycobacterial infection were reported among clients of one Australian salon.[1] France banned mesotherapy for fat removal briefly in 2011 and lifted the ban after investigators tied problems to unhygienic conditions rather than the method, while Brazil and some other South American countries have banned it for these purposes.[1]

No studies have been dedicated to pressurized mesotherapy for appearance beyond the single comparison with needle delivery noted above, and mesotherapy generally lacks standard clinical trials for cosmetic use.[1]

timeline.event: The term mesotherapy is coined by the French press.[1]
French Academy of Medicine recognizes mesotherapy as a specialty.[1]
